unique-paths.pattern: Grid DP: paths(r, c) = paths(r − 1, c) + paths(r, c − 1) (or one binomial coefficient)

approaches.name: Recursion over the last move
approaches.idea: The robot reaches cell `(r, c)` from the cell above or the cell to the left, so the number of paths is the sum of the paths to those two cells.
steps: `paths(r, c)`: if `r == 0` or `c == 0`, return 1 (a single straight line).
Otherwise return `paths(r − 1, c) + paths(r, c − 1)`.
Answer `paths(m − 1, n − 1)`.
approaches.why: Every path is traced separately, so the work is at least the answer itself (up to 2·10⁹ here).

approaches.name: 2-D table
approaches.idea: Fill `dp[r][c]` = paths to `(r, c)` row by row; the first row and column are all 1.
steps: For every other cell: `dp[r][c] = dp[r − 1][c] + dp[r][c − 1]`.
Return `dp[m − 1][n − 1]`.
approaches.why: Each of the m·n cells is computed once from two neighbours.

approaches.name: One row
approaches.idea: Each row only needs the row above. Keep one array: before the update `row[c]` is the value from above, and `row[c − 1]` is already the new value to the left.
steps: Set `row` to n ones.
Repeat for each of the remaining m − 1 rows: for `c` from 1, `row[c] += row[c − 1]`.
Return `row[n − 1]`.
approaches.why: Same number of steps; memory drops to a single row.

approaches.name: Count arrangements: C(m + n − 2, m − 1)
approaches.idea: Every path is a sequence of m − 1 downs and n − 1 rights in some order. The number of paths is the number of ways to choose which of the m + n − 2 moves are downs.
steps: Let `k = min(m, n) − 1` and `total = m + n − 2`.
Compute `C(total, k)` incrementally: `result = result · (total − k + i) / i` for `i = 1..k`.
Each intermediate value is an exact binomial coefficient, so the division is exact; use 64-bit numbers.
approaches.why: k multiplications and divisions. The intermediate product before dividing stays below about 2·10⁹ × 100, well inside 64 bits.

unique-paths-ii.pattern: Grid DP where blocked cells contribute 0 paths

approaches.name: Recursion that stops at obstacles
approaches.idea: Same as Unique Paths, but a blocked cell (or a cell off the grid) has 0 paths.
steps: `paths(r, c)`: return 0 if `r < 0`, `c < 0` or the cell is blocked; return 1 at `(0, 0)`.
Otherwise return `paths(r − 1, c) + paths(r, c − 1)`.
approaches.why: Every path is traced separately.

approaches.name: 2-D table
approaches.idea: Fill `dp[r][c]` row by row: 0 for obstacles, otherwise the sum of the values above and to the left.
steps: `dp[0][0] = 1` if the start is free, else 0.
For every cell: if blocked, 0; else add `dp[r − 1][c]` (if `r > 0`) and `dp[r][c − 1]` (if `c > 0`).
Return the bottom-right value.
approaches.why: One pass over the grid. Obstacles can make counts at middle cells larger than the final answer (even beyond 64 bits), so the sums wrap modulo 2³² on purpose: the final answer is below 2³¹, so the wrapped value is still exact. Java's `int` wraps by itself; C++ uses `unsigned` (signed overflow is undefined there) and JavaScript uses `>>> 0`.

approaches.name: One row
approaches.idea: Keep a single row: `row[c]` holds the value from above until it is updated; add the new value on its left, or reset it to 0 on an obstacle.
steps: `row[0] = 1` if the start is free.
For each grid row, for each `c`: if blocked, `row[c] = 0`; else if `c > 0`, `row[c] += row[c − 1]`.
Return `row[n − 1]`.
approaches.why: Same pass with one row of memory (and the same deliberate 32-bit wrap-around).

minimum-path-sum.pattern: Grid DP: cost(r, c) = grid[r][c] + min(cost from above, cost from the left)

approaches.name: Recursion over the last move
approaches.idea: The cheapest path to a cell comes from the cheaper of its top and left neighbours, plus the cell's own value.
steps: `cost(r, c)`: if out of the grid, return ∞; at `(0, 0)`, return `grid[0][0]`.
Return `grid[r][c] + min(cost(r − 1, c), cost(r, c − 1))`.
approaches.why: Overlapping subproblems are recomputed for every path.

approaches.name: 2-D table
approaches.idea: Fill `dp[r][c]` row by row from the same recurrence; the first row and column only have one way in.
steps: `dp[0][0] = grid[0][0]`; the first row and column are running sums.
Other cells: `dp[r][c] = grid[r][c] + min(dp[r − 1][c], dp[r][c − 1])`.
Return the bottom-right value.
approaches.why: Each cell once.

approaches.name: One row
approaches.idea: Keep one row of costs: `row[c]` is the cost from above until updated, and `row[c − 1]` is the new cost to the left.
steps: Fill `row` with the first row's running sums.
For each next grid row: `row[0] += grid[r][0]`; for `c >= 1`, `row[c] = grid[r][c] + min(row[c], row[c − 1])`.
Return `row[n − 1]`.
approaches.why: Same work, one row of memory.

triangle.pattern: Bottom-up DP: best(r, i) = value + min(best below-left, best below-right)

approaches.name: Recursion from the top
approaches.idea: From position `(r, i)`, the best path is its value plus the better of the two paths starting just below it.
steps: `best(r, i)`: on the last row, return the value.
Otherwise return `triangle[r][i] + min(best(r + 1, i), best(r + 1, i + 1))`.
Answer `best(0, 0)`.
approaches.why: Two calls per level for n levels, revisiting shared positions repeatedly.

approaches.name: Memoised recursion
approaches.idea: There are only about n²/2 positions; cache `best(r, i)` for each.
steps: Same recurrence as the brute force.
Store each position's result the first time it is computed and reuse it.
approaches.why: Each of the n(n + 1)/2 positions is solved once; the cache has the same size.

approaches.name: Bottom-up with one row
approaches.idea: Start from the bottom row and fold upwards: after processing row `r`, `row[i]` is the best path from `(r, i)` to the bottom. The top entry is the answer.
steps: Copy the last row into `row`.
For `r` from n − 2 up to 0, for `i` from 0 to r: `row[i] = triangle[r][i] + min(row[i], row[i + 1])`.
Return `row[0]`.
approaches.why: Each position once; going left to right is safe because `row[i]` only reads `row[i]` and `row[i + 1]`, which are still from the row below.

minimum-falling-path-sum.pattern: Row-by-row DP over three possible parents

approaches.name: Recursion from every starting cell
approaches.idea: From `(r, c)`, the best falling path is its value plus the best of the paths starting at the three cells below (those inside the grid). Try every cell of the first row.
steps: `best(r, c)`: on the last row, return the value.
Otherwise return `matrix[r][c] + min(best(r + 1, c + d))` over `d ∈ {−1, 0, 1}` inside the grid.
Answer the minimum of `best(0, c)` over all columns.
approaches.why: Up to three branches per row for n rows, from each of n starts.

approaches.name: Row-by-row DP with one row of memory
approaches.idea: Keep `prev[c]` = the cheapest falling path ending at column `c` of the previous row. Each cell of the next row adds its value to the cheapest of the up-to-three parents above.
steps: `prev` = the first row.
For each next row: `cur[c] = matrix[r][c] + min(prev[c − 1], prev[c], prev[c + 1])` (ignoring parents outside the grid).
Set `prev = cur`; at the end return `min(prev)`.
approaches.why: n² cells with 3 parents each; two rows of n values.

maximal-square.pattern: Square DP: side(r, c) = 1 + min(top, left, top-left)

approaches.name: Grow a square from every cell
approaches.idea: Treat each `1` as a top-left corner and keep growing the square while the new bottom row and right column are all `1`s.
steps: For each cell with `1`, set `side = 1`.
While the square of `side + 1` fits and its new row and column are all `1`, increase `side`.
Keep the largest `side`; return `side²`.
approaches.why: k = min(m, n): each start can grow up to k times, checking up to 2k cells each time.

approaches.name: 2-D DP on the bottom-right corner
approaches.idea: `dp[r][c]` = side of the largest all-ones square whose bottom-right corner is `(r, c)`. It can extend the squares ending above, to the left and diagonally above-left only as far as the smallest of them.
steps: Use a table with an extra zero row and column.
Track the largest side; return its square.
approaches.why: One pass with O(1) work per cell.

approaches.name: Same DP with one row
approaches.idea: Each row of the table only needs the row above, plus the old value of the diagonal neighbour, which can be kept in a variable before it is overwritten.
steps: Keep `row[0..n]` and a variable `diag` (the value from up-left).
For each cell: save `old = row[c + 1]` (the value above); if `1`, `row[c + 1] = 1 + min(old, row[c], diag)`, else 0; then `diag = old`.
Reset `diag = 0` at the start of each row; track the best side.
approaches.why: Same pass, one row of n + 1 integers.

count-square-submatrices-with-all-ones.pattern: Square DP: the largest square ending at a cell also counts the smaller ones there

approaches.name: Check every square of every size
approaches.idea: For each top-left corner, grow the square one size at a time while its new edge cells are all ones, counting each size that works.
steps: For each cell with 1, grow `side` from 1 while the square fits and the new bottom row and right column are all 1.
Each successful size is one more square; add them up.
approaches.why: k = min(m, n): up to k sizes per corner with up to 2k edge checks each.

approaches.name: DP on the bottom-right corner, summing the sides
approaches.idea: With `dp[r][c]` = side of the largest all-ones square ending at `(r, c)` (as in Maximal Square), that cell is the bottom-right corner of exactly `dp[r][c]` squares: one of each size up to it. Sum the table.
steps: For each cell with 1: `dp[r][c] = 1` on the first row or column, else `1 + min(dp[r − 1][c], dp[r][c − 1], dp[r − 1][c − 1])`.
Add `dp[r][c]` to the total.
Return the total. (The matrix itself can store `dp`.)
approaches.why: One pass with O(1) work per cell; writing the values into the input avoids an extra table.

dungeon-game.pattern: Reverse grid DP: health needed on entering a cell, computed from the princess back to the start

approaches.name: Recursion on the health needed from each cell
approaches.idea: Working forwards fails (a path that looks good early may need more health later). Instead ask: entering `(r, c)`, how much health do I need to survive to the end? It is what the better next cell needs, minus this room's effect, but at least 1.
steps: `need(r, c)`: if out of the grid, return ∞.
At the princess's room: `max(1, 1 − dungeon[r][c])`.
Otherwise `max(1, min(need(r + 1, c), need(r, c + 1)) − dungeon[r][c])`.
Answer `need(0, 0)`.
approaches.why: Two calls per cell without remembering results.

approaches.name: 2-D table from the bottom-right
approaches.idea: Fill `dp[r][c]` (health needed on entering) from the princess's room backwards, using a border of ∞ with a 1 placed just right of and just below the end so the formula works there too.
steps: Make `dp` of size (m + 1) × (n + 1) filled with ∞; set `dp[m][n − 1] = dp[m − 1][n] = 1`.
For `r` from m − 1 down to 0, `c` from n − 1 down to 0: `dp[r][c] = max(1, min(dp[r + 1][c], dp[r][c + 1]) − dungeon[r][c])`.
Return `dp[0][0]`.
approaches.why: Each cell once.

approaches.name: One row, filled backwards
approaches.idea: Each row only needs the row below, so one array of n + 1 values is enough: `row[c]` holds the value from below until it is overwritten.
steps: `row` = n + 1 values of ∞, with `row[n − 1] = 1` before the last grid row.
For `r` from m − 1 down to 0, for `c` from n − 1 down to 0: `row[c] = max(1, min(row[c], row[c + 1]) − dungeon[r][c])`. `row[n]` stays ∞: there is no way out past the right edge.
Return `row[0]`.
approaches.why: Same pass with a single row of memory.

cherry-pickup.pattern: Two walkers moving together: DP over (step, row of walker 1, row of walker 2)

approaches.name: Every forward path, then the best return path
approaches.idea: Enumerate every right/down path from the top-left to the bottom-right. For each, pick up its cherries, then find the best return path on the remaining grid with a simple grid DP. (Taking the single best forward path first and then the best return path is NOT enough — the two trips must be planned together.)
steps: DFS over all forward paths avoiding thorns.
At the bottom-right, compute the best second trip with `best[r][c] = grid[r][c] + max(best from above, best from the left)` on the grid with the first path's cherries removed.
Answer = max over forward paths of (cherries on it + best second trip); 0 if no path exists.
approaches.why: The number of forward paths grows like 4ⁿ/√n, and each needs an O(n²) DP for the return trip. Only workable for tiny grids, but it shows why both trips must be decided together.

approaches.name: Two walkers at once: DP over (step, r1, r2)
approaches.idea: The return trip reversed is just another top-left → bottom-right path, so send two walkers forward together. After `t` steps each is on the anti-diagonal `r + c = t`, so the state is `(t, r1, r2)`. When both stand on the same cell, its cherry counts once.
steps: `dp[r1][r2]` = most cherries with walker 1 at `(r1, t − r1)` and walker 2 at `(r2, t − r2)`; −∞ if impossible. Start: `dp[0][0] = grid[0][0]` at `t = 0`.
For `t` from 1 to 2n − 2: for each pair of rows, skip thorns and out-of-grid cells; take the best of the four previous pairs (each walker came from up or left).
Add the cherries at both cells (once if they are the same cell).
Answer `max(0, dp[n − 1][n − 1])` after the last step.
approaches.why: 2n − 1 steps × n² row pairs with 4 transitions each; only the previous step's n × n table is kept.

longest-increasing-path-in-a-matrix.pattern: DFS + memoisation on a DAG (or Kahn-style peeling)

approaches.name: DFS from every cell, no memory
approaches.idea: From each cell, explore every strictly increasing path with DFS and keep the longest.
steps: `dfs(r, c)` = 1 + the maximum of `dfs` over neighbours with a larger value (or 1 if there are none).
Call `dfs` from every cell and return the maximum.
approaches.why: The same cell is re-explored from every path that reaches it. On a "snake" grid where one path visits all 40,000 cells, the work is quadratic or worse, so it times out on the large test.

approaches.name: DFS with memoisation
approaches.idea: The longest path starting at a cell never changes, and increasing paths cannot loop. Cache each cell's answer the first time it is computed.
steps: `memo[r][c] = 0` means "not computed yet".
`dfs(r, c)`: if cached, return it; otherwise compute 1 + the best `dfs` of larger neighbours, store it and return it.
Return the maximum over all cells.
approaches.why: Each cell is computed once and looks at four neighbours. The graph "smaller → larger neighbour" is a DAG, so memoisation is safe. Recursion can go m · n levels deep on a snake-shaped grid, which needs a large stack (the judge provides one).

approaches.name: Peel layers by out-degree (Kahn)
approaches.idea: Count, for each cell, how many neighbours are larger. Cells with none are path ends. Remove them layer by layer; the number of layers is the longest path.
steps: For every cell, `out[r][c]` = number of strictly larger neighbours. Queue every cell with `out == 0`.
Process the queue one layer at a time. For each cell, decrement `out` of every strictly smaller neighbour, queueing those that reach 0.
Return the number of layers processed.
approaches.why: This is a topological sort of the DAG run from the sinks backwards: a cell is released only after every longer continuation has been counted, so its layer number equals the longest path starting there. No recursion, so no stack-depth worries.
